status: reviewed 2026-10-15 (hand review of the items; threshold calibrated on gpt-4.1, checked on Sonnet 5.5, see threshold_status)

match.method: best cosine similarity between each item (title + description) and each generated threat (name + description), BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5 embeddings
match.threshold_status: calibrated 2026-10-15 on 3 hand-graded gpt-4.1 runs (59 graded pairs, 36 negatives); checked 2026-10-17 on 3 hand-graded Sonnet 5.5 (Bedrock) runs, kept for both families (no per-family threshold): at 0.81 Sonnet had 0 false positives and 12 misses of 54 positives, but only 1 negative, so the false-positive side rests on gpt-4.1. Recall for Claude models is approximate (the matcher counted 16/15/14 against hand counts of 18/16/20, so up to 6 items per run, mostly under-counting; some misses are offset by partial matches scoring above 0.81, e.g. a generic leaked-HMAC-key threat matching MD-19 at 0.84). Other models, including GPT-6, are unchecked

items.title: SSRF via partner-controlled webhook URL
items.description: The worker POSTs to a webhook URL the partner registers; without blocking internal addresses, DNS rebinding and redirects, an attacker makes the worker request internal services (metadata endpoint, Redis, admin API).

items.title: Malicious image exploits sharp/libvips parsing
items.description: A crafted upload triggers a vulnerability in libvips or one of its codecs inside the resize worker, giving code execution or a crash in the worker container.

items.title: Decompression or pixel bomb exhausts the worker
items.description: A small file that decodes to an enormous image (or many frames) exhausts worker memory or CPU and stalls the resize queue.

items.title: Upload flooding fills storage and the job queue
items.description: A partner, or a stolen token, submits many uploads up to the 25 MB cap, filling the object store and the Redis queue and delaying other partners' jobs.

items.title: Cross-partner access via upload IDs or object keys (IDOR)
items.description: Where an upload ID or object key is dereferenced (signed-URL issuance, status lookup by upload ID), ownership isn't checked against the authenticated partner, so one partner reads another partner's images or metadata.

items.title: Signed URL leakage exposes private images
items.description: Short-lived signed URLs leak through logs, Referer headers, or webhook payloads and give anyone holding them access to private images until they expire.

items.title: Cross-partner leakage on the WebSocket status channel
items.description: Subscriptions to the ws channel aren't scoped to the authenticated partner, so a subscriber receives other partners' processing events and object keys.

items.title: JWT signing secret compromise enables token forgery
items.description: If the per-environment JWT signing secret leaks, an attacker mints valid bearer tokens for any partner.

items.title: Forged webhook deliveries via a leaked HMAC secret
items.description: A leaked webhook HMAC secret lets an attacker send forged completion notifications that partners accept as genuine.

items.title: Webhook replay
items.description: Signed webhook payloads with no timestamp or nonce can be captured and replayed to the partner.

items.title: Worker trusts job contents from the Redis queue
items.description: The worker acts on job fields (object key, partner ID, webhook target) without integrity checks, so anything that can enqueue, such as a compromised API container or injected job data, steers it at another partner's object or a different webhook.

items.title: Dead-letter queue: lost, replayed or poisoned webhook jobs
items.description: Webhook jobs that fail 5 retries move to a dead-letter queue; without monitoring, bounds and integrity checks they're silently lost, grow without limit, or are replayed later with stale or altered payloads.

items.title: Retry storm against partner endpoints
items.description: Exponential-backoff retries to a slow or attacker-controlled webhook endpoint tie up workers or amplify traffic toward a third party.

items.title: Admin UI authorization or session compromise changes partner settings
items.description: A hijacked partner admin session, or a missing authorization check on the admin UI, lets an attacker change the registered webhook URL or rotate the API key.

items.title: If the secrets-manager policy isn't scoped per container, compromising one exposes both keys
items.description: deployment.png draws the JWT key for the API and the HMAC key for the worker separately; if the policy lets either container read both, compromising one container exposes the JWT signing key and the HMAC key together.

items.title: Supply-chain compromise of a build or runtime dependency
items.description: A malicious release of a dependency (esbuild's install hook, sharp's prebuilt binaries, axios, jsonwebtoken) runs attacker code at install time or in the bundle that ships to both containers.

items.title: Content-type spoofing or polyglot files bypass validation
items.description: The zod schema checks the declared content type, not the bytes; a polyglot or mislabelled file reaches the worker or is served back with a dangerous type.

items.title: No audit trail for uploads, key changes and webhook deliveries
items.description: Without tamper-resistant logs of uploads, API-key rotation and webhook delivery outcomes, a partner can deny actions and incidents can't be reconstructed.

items.title: Shared webhook HMAC key lets one partner forge webhooks to others
items.description: HMAC is symmetric, so partners that verify signatures hold the key; with one webhook HMAC key for all partners (as deployment.png shows), any partner can forge signed deliveries to every other partner.

items.title: Container compromise exposes bucket-wide object-store credentials
items.description: The API and worker containers hold credentials to the object store, so compromising either exposes every partner's images, not just one partner's.

items.title: Partner API key theft, brute force or unthrottled token issuance
items.description: A partner API key can be stolen (admin UI, logs), guessed by brute force, or tried without limit because nothing throttles authentication attempts, giving the attacker that partner's access.
